maintopic: GOVERNMENT'S ACTION ON DRUG ABUSE-NATIONAL DRUG STRATEGY
GOVERNMENT'S ACTION ON DRUG ABUSE-NATIONAL DRUG STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Government has clearly demonstrated its commitment to combating drug abuse in Canada, with a new five-year plan announced yesterday. I wish to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) on this comprehensive action plan.
For years Canadians have expressed concern over drug abuse. Unfortunately, they have not known where to get accurate information, or where to turn for support and assistance when dealing with drug related problems.
The federal Government has taken a leadership role in educating Canadians on this social menace with the Action on Drug Abuse plan. I know that these measures will give parents in Canada hope for a better future for their children.
The national PRIDE office located in my riding, a drug education organization comprised of parents, teachers and police, has witnessed drug abuse by children at the elementary school level.
I might add that last week it had its national convention in Saskatoon, attracting over 1,600 people from across Canada. PRIDE estimates that nearly 600 children have dropped out of school in Saskatoon, a majority of these cases a result of drug abuse.
Attacking drug abuse is not only important for the preservation of our society as a whole but it is important for those Canadians who may, like these children, become victims of drugs. It is for these children that I give my fullest support to the plan of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

subtopic: DEPLETION OF OZONE LAYER-PARLIAMENT URGED TO ABOLISH USE OF STYROFOAM CUPS
DEPLETION OF OZONE LAYER-PARLIAMENT URGED TO ABOLISH USE OF STYROFOAM CUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will know, as other Members know, that growing attention is being paid to what is known as the depletion of the ozone layer.
Although I know that Governments are working in a coordinated fashion around the world to arrive at the policies and steps which need to be taken, one thing we could do right now would be to diminish the production and consumption of commodities and substances associated with the depletion of the ozone layer. One of those commodities is known as foam plastics or styrofoam.

May 26, 1987
I ask all Hon. Members to consider that Parliament and many other institutions across the country contribute to the problem of the depletion of the ozone layer by persistent use of styrofoam cups and foam plastic containers.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and other Members of the House to consider whether or not in the very short future we, as the House of Commons, the Parliament of Canada, could set an example for what Canadians could do collectively and individually in the short term in respect of this environmental problem, and consider the use of alternatives in this case.

subtopic: ARRIVAL OF DAN YLO SHUMUK IN CANADA-ROLE PLAYED BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
ARRIVAL OF DAN YLO SHUMUK IN CANADA-ROLE PLAYED BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many years the imprisonment of Mr. Danylo Shumuk, a Ukrainian dissident, was a matter of concern in the House. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and other Members of Parliament, including myself, brought his plight to the attention of the Canadian people and the Soviet authorities on many occasions.
Mr. Shumuk was the longest prisoner of conscience in history, having spent over 40 years in Nazi and Soviet prison camps.
This past Saturday I had the pleasure of welcoming Mr. Shumuk to Canada on behalf of the Canadian Government. He will be living with his nephew and family in Lumby, a community in my riding of Okanagan North.
Upon his arrival, Mr. Shumuk acknowledged publicly his debt of gratitude to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and particularly to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as well as to other Members of Parliament who supported his cause. He said:
I came to Canada because freedom is the very essence of life. I have
abandoned my own country. 1 came because I was not free. I am here because,
despite all my losses, I gained freedom which means everything to me.
Members of this House can be proud of the role they played in helping Mr. Shumuk achieve that freedom.

Mr. Speaker, on Sunday, May 24, the Child-Find organization released 15,000 balloons
in Montreal on the occasion of National Missing Children's Day. A photograph of a missing child was attached to each balloon. Several fathers and mothers launched balloons bearing photographs of their own children. The release of these balloons was a very moving moment for all who took part in a ceremony that was repeated in all Canadian communities where Child-Find is represented.
Mr. Speaker, sad to say, a considerable proportion of missing children are children who have been abducted by their own parents. Abduction of a child is illegal and should not be condoned, whether by strangers or by a divorced parent.
Although the Divorce Act has been amended, it does not have enough clout to prevent this kind of thing from happening. We think it is important for the Government to act with greater firmness in this area.
I therefore urge the Government to act quickly to enforce the new Divorce Act more rigorously, in order to stop the abduction of children, and I also recommend setting up followup and support programs for the parents of missing children.

subtopic: RECOMMENDATION CONTAINED IN REPORT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
RECOMMENDATION CONTAINED IN REPORT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning Jim MacNeill, Secretary General for the World Commission on Environment and Development, appeared before the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry. We discussed what Canada can do in the implementation of the Commission's report.
For instance, Canada can speak strongly in favour of the implementation of the recommendations when the General Assembly of the United Nations meets next October. Or, the Government can have the report examined by each federal Department and agency. Such a review may reveal policies that are not sustainable. For example, on energy we might find out that instead of promoting fossil fuel combustion, namely, coal, gasoline and the like, we should instead promote energy efficiency and the use of renewable sources of energy. Or, take agriculture. We may find that Canada's existing policies are incompatible with sustainable development as indicated already by the Senate report on soils. Or, take the flow of Canada's foreign aid. We may discover that the quality of assistance needs to be substantially improved in order to sustain development.
I urge the Government of Canada to elevate the environment and sustainable development to the centre of the decision-making process if we are to ensure economic growth for generations to come.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH STANDING ORDER 99(2)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises from a statement by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) in this House on May 15, 1987. I served notice on you, Mr. Speaker, as soon as possible following the statement of the Minister.
The question of privilege I will try to present here this afternoon arises from certain statements made by the Minister on May 15.
First, on March 19, 1987, the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration tabled its report in the House. At the very end of that report the committee indicated to the House and the Government that the committee requested that the Government respond to this report in accordance with Standing Order 99(2). Standing Order 99(2) reads as follows:
Within 120 days of the presentation of a report from a standing or special committee, the government shall, upon the request of the committee, table a comprehensive response thereto.
1 draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the operative word, "comprehensive".
Having said that, I want to point out that on May 15, the Minister tabled his letter to the chairman of the Standing Committee in which he said that, "the Standing Committee has suggested that we consider the recommendations as a package and we have done so".
There is nothing in the Standing Committee report that asks or even suggests that the Minister deal with that report as a package. There is no package deal. In fact, the Standing Committee's report to the House and the Government asked that the Government respond under Standing Order 99(2). We wanted a comprehensive response.
Furthermore, the only mention of the Standing Committee in the Minister's statement appears on page 8 of the statement where he said:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take this opportunity to thank each member of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration for their work on the Unemployment Insurance Program.
Their report was most helpful in our consideration of not only the current program but the other proposals for reform we received.
The committee suggested we consider its recommendations as a package and we have done so.
I am tabling today a letter to the Chairman of the Standing Committee reflecting the contents of my statement which will serve as the Government's response to the Report in accordance with the Standing Orders.
In other words, the Minister said that his statement of May 15 is to be considered the comprehensive response to the Standing Committee.
First, we did not ask for a package deal or for a package consideration. Second, we asked that the Minister and the Government respond under Standing Order 99(2) which calls for a comprehensive response.
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez
Furthermore, as recorded at page 6145 of Hansard of May 15, 1987, the Minister said:
In the past six months the Government has considered carefully the advice of all of the commissioners. As well we have studied the recommendations of the Royal Commission in Newfoundland, the Macdonald Commission recommendations and those of the Standing Committee. Members of this House will know that there are sharp and irreconcilable differences among these studies.
Again, that is a false statement. In fact, the Standing Committee made a comparison between the Standing Committee's recommendations and the Forget Commission's recommendations, and that study was available to the Minister. I have it here and I will table it so that the Minister may peruse it if he has not yet seen it. We found that there were 22 areas in which we reached agreement. There was no disagreement between Forget, Macdonald and the Standing Committee on 22 areas. When the Minister said that there were irreconcilable differences, he knew not of which he spoke.
We asked for a comprehensive response. Let me take a look at some of the recommendations. We recommended that there be a common entrance requirement of 10 weeks of insurable employment. Was there a comprehensive response to that in the Minister's statement? We recommended that a common two-week period be retained. Was there a comprehensive response to that recommendation? We recommended that the benefits remain at 60 per cent of weekly insured earnings but that the possibility of phasing in an increase of up to sixty-six and two-thirds per cent in the future be explored by the new commission. There was no comprehensive response to that recommendation. We recommended that the waiting period be eliminated entirely for maternity and adoption benefits. Was there a comprehensive response to that recommendation in the Minister's statement? No way. We recommended that the current practice be retained for work-sharing arrangements. Was there a comprehensive response to that in the Minister's statement? No way. I am simply picking some examples out to build a case, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
This morning, Mr. Speaker, we began today's opposition debate on the postal service in Canada. To us Liberals the postal service is very important, and we have shown this earlier today when the Right Hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) set the tone for this very important debate to express the views of the Liberal Party on the Canadian postal service.
Of course the position of the Minister responsible for Canada Post has been a great disappointment to me. Instead of taking this opportunity to unveil new measures to establish fair postal services he did nothing but level criticism at the Official Opposition, asking us to be responsible when in fact he himself has taken irresponsible action in the past few weeks, Mr. Speaker. Not so long ago the President of Canada Post stated-we must remember, Mr. Speaker, the context of very tense labour negotiations when he made his speech-the President of Canada Post said: "Strike or no strike, we will deliver the mail." A few days later the Minister responsible for Canada Post endorses the position of the President of Canada Post.
So, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister responsible-in this context, irresponsible might be more fitting-for Canada Post is asking us in the Opposition to be responsible, I wonder to what extent he understands what is at stake here, the seriousness of the situation facing us today when, in a few weeks and possibly sooner, our postal service may come to a full stop.
Mr. Speaker, in order to set the record straight, I will begin with the second reading debate on the Bill which established the Canada Post Corporation. In this regard, I refer to the Debates of the House of Commons of October 24, 1980, page 4075. At that time the Postmaster General, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) said, and I quote:
Had management explained more clearly to the employees what it intended to do, had it involved the employees in the change, had it guaranteed, from the very start, everyone's job security, the employees would have understood that the machines were not meant to replace them but rather to help them in their work, and union leaders would have taken part in the operation rather than opposing it.
In the same speech, he added:
Crown corporation status will not remedy all our ills or difficulties. Every organization, be it government or industry, faces normal operational problems. However, with the streamlining of many of the facets of our operations and the support and good will of the employees, the Canada Post Corporation will be able to provide all Canadians with the postal service to which they are entitled and which they deserve. I want now to reiterate what I have said-
Those are the words of the former Minister.
-publicly and privately to union representatives, that is, I intend to have union representatives on the board of directors in order that they can get directly involved and participate fully in the good administration of the corporation.
That is the spirit in which the Canada Post Corporation was established in 1980-81, Mr. Speaker. It was precisely in the spirit of a full co-operation between management and staff. No modern and aggresive business can implement a successful corporate plan without a full co-operation between management and employees.
We only have to look at facts, Mr. Speaker. Since 1981, there was no strike. The reduction of the deficit was one of the goals, as well as to provide a better service and improve labour relations. Even as regards the reduction of the deficit, Canada Post made improvements since 1981 and the corporation improved its services in some areas.
But in 1984, Mr. Speaker, Conservative Members tried to imitate the Liberals during the election campaign and they promised the moon, the earth and everything else. But once in Government, they took off their masks, became real Conservatives and started to cut in services.
The excuse was that these cuts had to be made for the sake of deficit reduction, Mr. Speaker. We are very much aware of the problem and we agree on the necessity to work towards that reduction. However, we must not place the burden on ordinary people only, on those who are less fortunate than others, but we must call upon everybody. Mr. Speaker, what have we seen since 1984? Those who have been called upon to reduce the deficit are older people, handicapped people and small business people who have no alternative but to use Canada Post, whereas larger businesses can well afford private couriers ... It is a truism to say that if postal workers go on strike, small businesses will be the first ones to be penalized. Mr. Speaker, these people will suffer because the Government, by not allowing Canada Post enough time to reduce its deficit, will be forcing a strike, and these groups will bear the brunt.
However, again for the sake of reducing the deficit, the Government had no hesitation in guaranteeing bank deposits over $60,000 in two Western banks. Of course, no small businesses had deposits over that amount, Mr. Speaker. Nevertheless, the Government did not hesitate, despite the fact that the operation cost us perhaps six or seven times the amount of the Canada Post deficit. I could give lots of examples, such as the Reisman Brothers case, the Port-Cartier penitentiary and so on. We know that in many instances this Government has been squandering public funds! But it has to make cuts when ordinary Canadians, and a service that
May 26, 1987

everybody needs are concerned. I would hate to forget as well the Old Age Security pensions de-indexation.
So, Mr. Speaker, if the Government wants to reduce the deficit, it must ask all Canadians to tighten their belts. But in the case of Canada Post, only the elderly, the small businesses, the handicapped, the housewives, will suffer from the poor postal service resulting from the policy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who said in his 1986 Budget that Canada Post must get rid of its deficit and balance its books by 1988.
Mr. Speaker, just this morning, my Leader, the Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition, said that it took the United States 14 years to achieve that result. But in Canada, a country so diversified, with only 25 million people and a territory larger than the United States, we want to reach in four to five years an objective that the Americans took 14 years to achieve. It is not good enough, Mr. Speaker. But in that case, the Minister of Finance decided to axe expenditures at Canada Post, and the management of the Corporation-under the direction of the Minister, has decided to cut the services, and we see the results.
Canadians are not satisfied with the service. We cut the door-to-door delivery by installing supermailboxes which are far from being "super", Mr. Speaker; they open by themselves, one key can open many of them, and there are also snow removal problems. Not long ago, a committee showed us pictures of the supermailboxes which had been installed for four to five months, and they were in a poor state. After only four to five months . . . Imagine how durable these boxes are! Just this morning, in response to a question, the Minister said that the investment will be paid for in four to five years thanks to all the savings made.
Mr. Speaker, we must analyse and put into perspective a number of things; since the effects of savings cannot be felt immediately, cuts have to be made. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from the March 25, 1987 editorial of Le Droit, dealing with Canada Post Corporation:
How important is postal service in our society? If one is to believe the complaints of users, it is one of the rare issues which concerns everybody-the role of the postal service is similar to that of public transit, but it is of greater importance. After all, some people never take the bus or the train, but very few people do not receive mail.
However, given the size of its operating budget, Canada Post-is the least costly among Crown corporations. Given that the Government has had to provide 184 million dollars to Canada Post in 1985-86 fiscal year and that this accounts for only 6,2 percent of its operating budget, one is led to believe that no other Crown corporation of comparable scale (60,000 employees) has been able to match such a performance in modern day Canada ...
In the case of Canada Post, the federal Treasury has never had to finance more than 12 percent of the corporation's budget since it has become a Crown corporation, on October 16, 1981. In fact, the Government's share has gone from 10,3 percent in 1982-83 to 6,2 percent in 1985-86. The Federal Government contribution increased up until fiscal 1984-85-the 12 percent high previously mentioned-after which it decreased, as we know. However, in the face of such satisfactory performance on the part of a Crown corporation, the Federal Government is acting as if Canada Post should bring in the same kind of dividends as are to be expected from the sale of beer, wine or lottery tickets. In a country as vast as ours, the postal service must be considered an essential service and, as such, it should be managed in strict conformity with the committments undertaken by Government under the enabling legislation.

We therefore have, Mr. Speaker, in the March 25 editorial of the Ottawa newspaper Le Droit dealing with Canada Post Corporation, a clear indication of the type of Canadian postal service corporation which Canadians would like to see.
Mr. Speaker, with the Government's authorization, the Canada Post Corporation has reduced service not only in cities, but also in rural areas, that is to say, in both larger and smaller centres. Of course, everybody has heard about the closing of post offices in rural areas. Travelling from coast to coast in Canada, I have had the opportunity to hear just how concerned Canadians are about the Government's intention to get rid of these small post offices which were the very soul of villages.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to describe how we, as Liberals, see post offices in rural areas. And I quote:
"In small towns and villages, the post office remains the establishment most frequently visited by local people. It easily becomes an information centre for the whole community. That is where people go to get information on such matters as social services and obtain income tax returns, as well as scholarship and job application forms. Postmasters often serve as resource people. The federal Government is present everywhere in Canada, and the post office remains a familiar place which brings the Government down to the dimension of man. The post office is a universal meeting place. It creates links in the community. It is a unifying force which gives the community and each and every one of its members a feeling of belonging."
This is how we see post offices in rural areas, in small villages, Mr. Speaker. I was quoting from a statement made by the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), the former Postmaster General.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are quite concerned about what is going to happen to their post offices. They are also quite concerned about what is going to happen to their postal services. Every morning when they open their newspapers, in whatever language it is printed, they read about threats of strikes. Instead of acting as a mediator and trying to calm apprehensions, the Government throws oil on the fire and says: We have to be tough, we have to be rough, we have to crush the workers because we must carry out this plan which calls for the elimination of nearly 8,000 jobs.
Well, as I was saying at the very beginning, Mr. Speaker, for a corporate plan to be applicable, accepted and successfully carried out, you need the co-operation of both the administrators and employees. For the time being, the Canada Post Corporation has not obtained this co-operation. Quite the contrary. Together with the Government, it has sought confrontation by presenting its corporate plan without consultation. It has also taken action which is contrary to the spirit of co-operation on which the postal service was based at the time of its creation. When we were in Government, we, Liberals, had promised to have labour representatives on the board of the Canada Post Corporation for the very purpose of

creating the spirit of co-operation needed for a harmonious work relationship, to fulfil the mandate of ensuring a better postal service, reducing the deficit and maintaining a fair climate of labour relations.
Mr. Speaker, we have to be aware that we shall never have a good postal service if confrontation between labour and management does not stop. Up till this morning, on this opposition day, the Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation had the opportunity to give a clear signal to both parties by saying: "Let's sit down, please. Let's talk. Let's settle the problems. Let's see how it could be done. We could delay the privatization plan." That is the recommendation of the Marchment report which the Minister quoted this morning, but only the parts that suited him. Indeed, he did not say for example that the Marchment report recommends to wait till 1990 before considering the privatization of Canada Post, for it is only at the project stage, Mr. Speaker. He wants to privatize all retail outlets. He wants to install superboxes so that mail can be delivered by private contractors. Now do you think the Corporation's 60,000 employees will say: "Yes, Mr. Minister, because you want to reduce the deficit, we will do that at once!" It will have to be worked out through the negotiation process, with common sense and a lot of time. It took the Americans 14 years to work it out. But here, with only 25 million people, in a country as diverse and as vast as Canada, we want results within five years, Mr. Speaker.
It shows how unrealistic this Convervative Government is. Ever since they took office the small guy has had to pay while the rich always get more.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, today we condemn the Government for creating a situation that could lead to violent confrontation. Why violent? Let me explain. 1 have in front of me a press release issued by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.

In its press release this morning, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business asked Gallup to conduct a poll to see whether or not Canadians wanted a postal strike. I am not surprised by the results.
Everybody in Canada wants the mail delivered. They do not care about a strike or the deficit; they want mail delivered. That is what is important, and the Government does not understand it.
The Government is using the confrontational method because it wants to reduce the deficit. The Canada Post Corporation was doing okay until the Minister of Finance said: "You have to balance your books in fiscal 1988".
It took 14 years for them to balance their books in the United States, and they want it done in Canada in five years.
I see you indicating, Mr. Speaker, that my time is expiring. Mr. John Bulloch said in the press release this morning that Canadians simply want the mail to get through and that they
do not want to be used as pawns in a show-down with the forces, the forces being the Government, Canada Post management, and the union.
Canadians want their mail delivered. They want door-to-door service. They want to keep the rural post office as an identity, as a symbol of Canadian unity. I ask the Government and the Minister responsible for Canada Post to stop this confrontational attitude undertaken a few months ago, sit down with management and labour and come up with a plan acceptable to Canadians, workers and management.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to my colleague, the critic for the Post Office, who I think speaks knowledgeably and passionately about this issue. He has been at the forefront in trying to bring some sense into the Post Office.
When he talks about having the mail delivered not only door-to-door but as a unified service across the country I think he is hitting a significant nail right on the head, the same one that Canadians from coast-to-coast want the Government to understand.
What about a community with a postman, a postwoman or a postperson who delivers mail on one side of the street and then crosses over and does not? What kind of citizenship is this? There is only one kind of citizenship and that is first class citizenship.
But what about the person in the a subdivision who asks why the Government rationalizes not delivering door-to-door because of financing when that new subdivision gets an entirely new infrastructure from other levels of Government, new schools, new churches, new recreation facilities and new transportation arteries? Why is the Post Office different? Perhaps the buck is being passed to the municipalities. The Government is saying that the municipalities are not telling us in advance when these new subdivisions are being created. Therefore, the Post Office has no way of budgeting for them. I would like the comments of the Hon. Member, who has been very much involved in terms of the inequities this creates within a community and between communities vis-a-vis the concept of the supermailbox and whether it is economically efficient. Or is it almost the same when you consider the cost of having to maintain those supermailboxes vis-a-vis the fixing and the replacing of them?

1 want to thank my colleague for the question, Mr. Speaker. In the past we had green boxes. Whether there was a lack of co-operation or a problem in management, the Post Office was unable to absorb all the new communities that sprang up so rapidly. Past policy was to have green boxes so people could receive their mail at the corner of the street on a temporary basis until the Post Office could organize the delivery route and install door to door delivery.
May 26, 1987

Some Members go around saying that the supermailbox is Liberal policy. I invite anyone to come to my riding of St. Leonard. It was built in the last 15 or 20 years. The only streets without door-to-door delivery are those built in late 1984, 1985 and 1986. My own house was built in 1983-84. I have home delivery. Two streets away people do not. I took a walk this week-end and 1 found not far from my house supermailboxes on a continuation of an existing street. Because the continuation of the street was built in 1985, people who live on that continuation do not have door-to-door delivery. That is the kind of discrimination that Canadians do not want to take. They are right. They pay the same taxes whether municipal, provincial or federal. Everyone pays 36 cents for a stamp. If one has to register a letter, one pays the same price whether or not one has home delivery. We are creating second-class citizens.
We have a deficit problem and we should face it rationally. Management and unions should sit down to try to improve performance in the Post Office, but not by way of confrontation. We must leave confrontation to the 1970s because we know the results of it. Canada Post Corporation was created in 1981 to avoid the confrontation which the Conservative Government and the new management of Canada Post is creating right now.

Since there are no banks situated in the community, we are required to deal with banks in Red Rock or Nipigon, both approximately 25 miles to the east or in Thunder Bay, 45 miles to the west. Most banking transactions are carried out by mail due to the travelling distances and costs involved with personal attendance. Money orders are purchased with all cash coming into the municipal offices.
Quite often, especially during tax collection periods, there may be thousands of dollars collected weekly which must be mailed to the bank ... The loss of the rural post office would be a great inconvenience. I would be required to travel great distances to the nearest post office to purchase postage supplies and pick up registered mail.
That letter was written by Mrs. Helena Tamminen, Secretary-Treasurer, Township of Dorion, Ontario, and sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on December 22, 1986. speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this point in the debate introduced by the Opposition, a debate of course that is of concern to all Canadian citizens, that may concern them because as the Hon. Member stated a few minutes ago, they want to sow fear in the hearts of people for political gains.
What I would like to do at this point, Mr. Speaker, is perhaps make a historical review of the Canada Post Corporation, or the Canadian postal service.
The postal service as we know it today started in the mid-19th century. It was established to meet the needs in terms of exchange of information felt by the business and industrial world and by that increasing part of the public that could read and write.
Since then, tremendous changes happened and the postal service is just as essential today as it was before the invention of the telephone, the computer, the airplane and the communications satellite. But if it is to survive, it will have as any other service to adapt to a changing, modern world.
When the postal service was inaugurated in Canada during the 1850s, most Canadians were living in rural areas, on the farm and in small towns. Today, although rural Canada remains an important component, the great majority of Canadians live in major cities or suburbs.
At the beginning of the postal service, manpower was inexpensive. People worked long hours for a small salary, which meant businesses could allow a high labour content while selling their goods and services at competitive prices. People had no automobiles and public transportation did not exist. In order to pick up or mail their letters, they had to either walk or harness.
Today, they drive to the stores, the supermarkets, or they drop their mail in mail boxes at their jobs. That postal service really did not change. But such is not the case of other service industries.
Nowadays, people won the right to a much better salary for significantly reduced work hours, so that productivity must be increased if costs are to be controlled.
The Canada Post Corporation has a mandate to bring the Canadian postal service into the world of the 21st Century.
This means to alter traditional procedures for the provision of a postal service and we know that any such change is not easy. However, the Corporation has undertaken to abide with a fundamental principle in the modernization and adjustment of postal services in Canada. It is to make sure that all Canadians wherever they live enjoy a reliable and cheap postal service. Methods will perhaps change. It is possible that partnership arrangements with private sector which are as old as postal services themselves will be further altered. However, the postal service,thanks to imaginative solutions, will always meet the needs of future generations of Canadians.
It should be noted that the Corporation has promised to give a 90-day notice of any change made to the rural service. The new plan of Canada Post will mean a better postal service for all Canadians.
When the Marchment Committee asked Canadians what they wanted more especially from their postal services, they clearly answered: reliability. The Corporation is improving its operations and modernizing its facilities so that Canadians may expect a reliable mail delivery service.Each year, there are 150,000 new addresses in Canada as more people are settling in new homes or are launching a new business. The Corporation will act quickly to provide a practical and economic service to those new addresses. It will put an end to the long file at the counters of the general delivery service where people have to pick up their mail and will remove the green community boxes which are rightly despised.
It will be much easier to buy stamps and other postal items. The Corporation will make use of the skills of the retail industry namely cornerstores, general stores, drugstores, and supermarkets, to sell stamps and to provide other postal services where people do their shopping and at times that are convenient to them. Furthermore, the number of outlets selling stamps and providing other postal services will increase by about 50 p. 100 within the next 10 years. That means that people will know where to go after 5 or 6 p.m. to buy stamps.
Canada Post will limit rate increases. In the future, the cost of mailing a letter will vary only according to inflation. There will be no more sudden and dramatic increases in the price of stamps. People will benefit from these improvements in the postal service without any tax increase.
Canada Post will be financially sound as any other business which offers a good service. In this way, people will not have to pay twice, first at the post office, and second through their income tax. There will be no more postal deficit to be added to the national debt which our children and grandchildren will have to pay back.
May 26, 1987

At this time the corporation has some 12,000 sales outlets where one can buy stamps and other postal products and services. This number is broken down as follows: 6,000 post offices manned by employees of the Corporation, 2,000 auxiliary offices operated by large and small businesses, and 4,000 agencies that sell stamps. The Corporation will increase the accessibility of its services. Therefore, the total number of outlets will increase by 50 per cent over a period of 10 years with better access to these outlets.
Nowadays, it happens quite frequently that post offices are not located in shopping areas. Several post offices were centrally located when they were built initially a few generations ago, but now due to shifts in population, businesses have moved somewhere else. Most of the time, post offices are open when it is the least convenient for working people to get there, and they are closed during the business hours of other retail stores. Existing post offices are also more likely to be located where parking is difficult than where there are lots of free parking spaces. Those are some of the reasons why the Corporation will more and more place retail sales into the hands of the private sector, of business people who are already serving the public by selling groceries, stationery items, drugs and all kinds of other products. Postal items could be sold in stores where people are going already.
Those businesses are already located where people make their provisions and are open longer hours than most post offices. In addition, they are usually located where it is easy to park a car as in shopping centers. Those measures are also based on sound management principles. The wages of those stores' employees are comparable to those of private sector businesses and the Corporation can increase the number or the quality of its retail outlets without having to build new postal offices facilities. We know that, in the end, those costs are borne by postal service users.
Improved service plans in rural areas of Canada undoubtedly mean that several forms of relationship with customers, some of which were established more than a century ago, will change gradually. So that those changes will be well understood by members of the communities concerned and that those people will be heard in the process, as I said earlier, Canada Post will give a 90-day notice of any change it is contemplating. That period will be used to consult people and their elected representatives before any change is implemented.
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post Corporation is improving rural service in several ways. One is to provide the supermailbox to its customers, which means that in small municipalities, people will no longer have to go to the Post Office nor to stand in line for the general delivery at limited business hours. They will just have to go to their supermailbox which will generally be closer to their homes, and to remove their parcels and their mail whenever it suits them.'According to a recent poll, 94 per cent of the people who tried the supermailbox are very pleased. This supermailbox gives them the same degree of safety and of
Supply
convenience as a rented postal box with a lock. The supermailbox however is free of charge. In addition to collecting your mail and your parcels, you can mail your letters in the supermailbox.
The Corporation would also increase the number of outlets where the people who live in rural areas will be able to buy stamps and other services. Their number will increase from 5,000 now to 7,000 within 10 years. These measures are part of a global plan aimed at improving access to the services offered by the Corporation through increased co-operation with the private sector. By increasing the number of those outlets in rural Canada, the Corporation will take advantage of the resources of local business people and entrepreneurs instead of using offices it would have to build or operate itself.
In many cases this will mean longer business hours and a more convenient location. At the present time, several post offices are open only from 30 to 40 hours a week. Private sector outlets are normally open much longer. These outlets of postal products and services operated by the private sector will be located where people go shopping, which will exempt them from having to stop in several places.
Again, Mr. Speaker, it must be reminded that that 90 days, advance notice will allow consultations with people and their representatives before those changes become effective.
The transition will not affect significantly those concerned. It will be spread over a long period of time so that the impact on employees could be alleviated through promotions, resignations and retirements.
It is to be reminded also that new business and employment opportunities will arise in Canadian rural communities from further co-operation with the private sector. Needless to say that those opportunities will be available as well to Canada Post employees. And they could also take advantage of new possibilities within the Corporation itself as new positions will be created to control private retail sale outlets.
Postal service expansion plans for a viable universal mail service at Canada Post are more important to rural Canadians than to their urban counterparts. Competitor operations, such as private couriers, have revolved around larger urban centres where there is more mail. Unlike Canada Post, those businesses are not required to provide a universal service to those little or less populated rural areas.
In the next decade, and possibly the following years, Canada Post will proceed with a comprehensive survey of the market for every future outlet. In fact, a market survey is mostly an analysis of preferences, of consumer requirements and needs, and such analyses are common practice in the private sector. They will determine what sites and services from coast to coast are suited to consumer needs and whether or not postal products and services should be made available on a given site. Before any decision is made, Canada Post will consider factors such as demand, clients, community preferences, parking lots as well as other existing retail sale outlets in the vicinity.

May 26, 1987
Supply
All these factors will help it choose the most practical place to locate these products and services. It must determine where customers work, and shop, and at what time they prefer to buy postal products. The goal of the Corporation is to increase and improve the quantity and the quality of its services to the benefit of the user.
Market surveys have been undertaken in nine medium-sized communities in Canada. The results will determine where and how postal services will be offered. The Canada Post Corporation will carefully study each location to make sure that customers will be better served. And if it wants to remain competitive, it must make it easier for its customers to buy its products and services. Post offices are more costly to operate in terms of salaries as well as in terms of capital expenditures and operating expenses required by this type of large obsolete buildings.
Franchising is an important feature in the new plan. Businesses will buy from Canada Post the right to sell postal products in a given area. They will also buy their stamps and other products at wholesale prices as for any other merchandise purchased for resale.
What is new is the relationships between the Corporation and private sector businesses which will be more similar to those between travel or car rental agencies and their franchisers. More services will be offered, working hours will be longer and will include evenings and week-ends, and sales outlets will be more conveniently located. The image of the Canada Post Corporation will be consistent and clearly posted. Sales outlets will be much more attractive and will project a lively commercial image from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The Corporation has already implemented a pilot project in Metropolitan Toronto and has announced another one for Winnipeg where it has to leave its rented accommodation. According to Canada Post, customer reaction was very encouraging. In both cities, all retail clerks affected by these new measures were or will be reassigned to local postal operations.
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post considers the welfare of its employees as an important part of its plan. As its business volume increases, it will be more capable of integrating its employees. But the goal of the Corporation is to increase and improve the quality and the quantity of its services to the benefit of users. It is very important that this service be centered on user's needs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one comment. The Hon. Member referred to a Canada Post policy calling for the closing of post offices. She referred to the famous 90 days, and I would like to emphasize now that in reality, Canada Post had difficulty in enforcing this regulation, and I am under the impression that it never took it seriously, until quite recently. The Standing Committee on Government Operations which addressed this problem came out with a
unanimous report which is so strong that it conveyed to the Canada Post Corporation the message that it should truly have a consultation process and a recommendation that individual post offices should be closed only when, after consultation, all the people involved agreed. However, when the people involved say that a post office should remain open, it should not be closed. In a way, this would be a veto given to the public. On the basis of the representations made to us, we did not feel that the Canada Post Corporation was properly applying the regulations. The Minister had announced following the tabling of the corporate plan . . .
Mr. Speaker, I have a question. The Hon. Member referred repeatedly to the fact that there would be more post offices, that this would give private enterprise an opportunity to develop postal services in their own corporations and commercial environment. So, instead of having a post office close at 6 p.m., there could be, for instance, on Thursdays and Fridays when stores are open until 9 p.m., so-called "extended" hours.
I would like the Hon. Member to tell us what she thinks of this point, on which even the Minister himself touched this morning. Now, in urban centres, there are small post offices located in drugstores, for instance. As a matter of fact, there is one in the building where I have my riding office and I can tell you that if I go down there to try and buy stamps or have a letter registered after 4.30 p.m., the door is closed. It closes even before the central post office which is located a little further away.
The Government would like to have us believe that, by turning over post offices to the private sector, we would have access to the post office almost 24 hours a day, but such is not the case. For the time being, at least, as she said, that is the way the Government would like it to be, but I think that this would mean a counter where stamps are sold, not a real post office where one could send a registered letter or a package.
I would like the Hon. Member to comment on this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand my hon. friend's concerns. He represents a riding just as I do. What we both want is for our fellow citizens to be well served.
Through this privatization of a new service, the purpose of which is to reduce administrative costs, it is clear that the little post office in the drug store which closes at 4 p.m. or 4.30 p.m. was not given a full franchise. It is because not so far away, there is another post office.
We say that when the post office as it now exists closes for any reason, including the fact that the postmaster has retired, we would transfer the services to the private sector, either in a convenience store, a drug store or a supermarket.
Because he will get paid a commission on the stamps he sells and the service he provides, the owner will be eager to stay open as long as possible during his business hours, and we all know how long convenience stores remain open. I think that people generally will benefit, because, after 5 p.m., instead of having to wait till the next day to buy stamps or do any other
May 26, 1987

business, they will be able to obtain service up to 6 p.m., 7 p.m. or 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my honourable friend. It refers to the privatization of post offices in urban areas, as well as the franchising policy. I would like her comments on three points.
First, is she aware that before this franchising policy, the Corporation had opened new offices, under new management, open longer hours? I mention this because these public post offices provided the same services as the private post offices. And one of the arguments in favour of this policy of privatization are the extended hours and greater access to the public. We could do the same with public post offices.
My second point is this: What is your reaction to the fact that by franchising post offices, the Government or Canada Post are going to lose revenues because it will only be possible to privatize profitable post offices as no businessman would accept to operate a post office which is losing money? This policy will translate into a loss of revenue for Canada Post and will have an impact on the deficit.
Also, I would like to know her opinion about the salaries of the people working in post offices. These people are now being paid $12 an hour while after privatization, they will be paid the minimum wage of $4.55 which, in a City like Toronto, is the poverty threshold. Will such a policy not reduce people to poverty?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the first question, the public post office versus the private post office, as far as customer or people service in concerned, certainly people will prefer... In fact, when you have a location in a small community, whether rural or semi-urban, where service is available for 12, 15 hours a day, people cannot help being satisfied, and they will have the same service.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext: But that is possible also with the public post office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs

speechtext:
Perhaps I did not understand correctly your first question, but anyway I will try to answer the second and third questions.
You say there will be a loss of income. Look, businessmen who need the service always go there, postal service will always be required. So they will have a choice. If they only want to buy stamps, they can always go to the convenience store or private services, but if they need something more involved like overseas mail, which perhaps the convenient store could not handle, there will always be the post office available to them. So, the income is there. I do not see how income will decline at the Canada Post Corporation.
Third, you refer to salaries. Well, it will be private enterprise, or private enterprise wages. There will be a fair balance just the same, if in the same service location an employee, whether assigned to paper supplies or produce, perhaps, if he is in a store and that right next to it. . . So, employees in the
Supply
same business will have competitive wages. I do not see why an employee assigned to the postal service would earn less than somebody else in the same store. After all, it is private enterprise.
As you know, all that privatization is aimed at saving Canada Post's money. Who is paying for that deficit? It is always the individual, always the taxpayer. Often, people come to my office and tell me: If the Government gave us such or such a service, we could have a subsidy for this or that. My first reaction, all I tell them initially is this: Look, if you are prepared to pay more taxes, O.K., we will give it to you. But each time you receive a service or a grant, it is with your tax money. We get it from your pocket. At that point people realize that it is really their tax money we are managing, and they may then be perhaps more reasonable in their representations, their expectations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the third time in the last few months this House is debating the condition of postal service in Canada. Today we are indebted to the Official Opposition for moving the motion condemning the Government for allowing the deterioration of Canada's postal service by undermining the principle of fair and equal service to all Canadians.
As a Member who represents a largely rural riding, there are certain points about postal service that concern me more than others. Today I want to address the closure of rural post offices and the closure of rural postal delivery routes, which I notice is not mentioned in the motion but which I am sure is implied by it. I also want to mention the situation of confrontational actions within the postal service, initiated by the board of Canada Post and initiated and covertly supported by the Government.
The situation with rural areas is one that I believe is comparable to the introduction of the supermailbox in suburban areas, but one where the potential consequences of the actions that have been taken are indeed for more serious in the case of the rural and smaller communities.
We have seen a history of actions taken by the Government that are intended to diminish and downgrade postal service and put Canada Post, both the unions and the corporation itself, in the position of being a scapegoat for other failures, including those of the Government.
We have seen the Government defended by its members on the Standing Committee on Government Operations. We have seen the committee adjourned for lack of a quorum when some members departed.
The Minister responsible for Canada Post was replaced in February of this year after a storm of protest. We have heard some favourable comments from the new Minister which, unfortunately, have not been translated into any action to

May 26, 1987
Supply
improve the conditions under which postal service is delivered in Canada.
The new Minister said that no closure of a rural post office or change in postal service will be undertaken. The Government said that postal service was more important than balancing the Budget by next year. However, we have not seen actions taken to put flesh on these skeletal commitments.
The committee's proposal that there should be consultation with local committees has apparently been discarded or at least devalued by the Minister saying that the final decision to close rural post offices or make other changes in rural mail service will be made by Canada Post. I respectfully submit that this response missed the point. I believe it is understood that the final decisions always lay with Canada Post. The problem was that Canada Post was not taking adequate notice of the users of the postal service or the representations of their elected representatives and their spokespeople.
I believe that it is incumbent upon Canada Post to consider very seriously the input that it receives when carrying out its responsibility to make the final decision with respect to the location.
The second report of the Government Operations Committee states: "Your committee is appalled by the heavy-handed approach taken by Canada Post in the past in its attempts to close certain rural offices. In many instances, consultation was totally lacking. It is your committee's view that rural communities deserve better treatment".
The committee went on to say: "Your committee realizes that demographic and other changes occurring in rural regions may occasionally result in the need for a post office closure or a change in postal service".
The committee recommended that in the future a minimum of 90 days' notice be given regarding each and every anticipated closure to allow for consultation to take place.
I understand that the Post Office has taken notice of that recommendation, apparently not through any good offices of the Government, but on the analysis that this was indeed the sensible, politic thing to do, as well as a fair and reasonable step to take within the context of a democratic society.
Of course, the values of information and consultation are dear to all Members of the House. They are values that cannot be translated into concrete effects unless Canada Post is willing to consider fully the information, the opinions, the wishes and the aspirations that are communicated to it by the users of the postal service.
I want to talk briefly about the situation of Canada Post being called upon to balance its budget. This objective was obviously placed on Canada Post unilaterally because there appeared to have been no consultations between the Government and Canada Post as to what might be a realistic, workable and viable business plan to enable Canada Post to reach that objective of full revenue dependency.
Of course, our system provides the Government with the right to impose such a decision, but such a right should be exercised with much more care than the Government evidently did in this case. Instead, it imposed this arbitrary deadline on Canada Post. In response to that deadline, Canada Post came up with a plan which some could scarcely describe as other than arbitrary, as is reflected in some of its objectives. Canada Post indicated that over 10 years it would close, amalgamate or privatize all of the 5,221 rural post offices. It proposed to eliminate rural lot line delivery to 100,000 customers.
Our Party believes that this plan is one that could not be considered by Canadians as providing a fair solution to the problem of the postal service paying for itself and making the appropriate changes to the postal service in order to meet the Government's deficit reduction objectives.
Privatizing 3,500 rural post offices would not be the answer. Replacing the post office with a stamp outlet in a pharmacy or a corner store will not compensate a community for the loss of such an essential institution as the post office, nor will it replace the service that the post office provides. Mail sorting would cease in rural communities. It would be further centralized. Jobs would be lost. Many secondary services which are presently operated would be obviously curtailed.
Moreover, a tradition would die. I believe that I was the first person to mention in the House that in some communities the post office is the only institution that flies the Canadian flag. I did so not to set up some form of sympathy-seeking image but simply to record in the House what I have observed in some places to be the fact.
The post office in many remote and rural communities is central to the ideal and the identity the residents of those communities, in their often widely dispersed outlying areas, feel in their identity as Canadians. In many ways the post office is the only tangible contact that some of them have with their Government. Thus it was that there was some resistance in rural communities to the idea of the post office even becoming a Crown corporation because it would mean that the link between the people and the Government would essentially be severed by the turning of Canada Post into a Crown corporation.
Some of the consequences that I have seen in my riding are obviously detracting from that relationship that should exist between every Canadian and the federal Government. I saw rural routes discontinued in Dinorwic, in Pine Wood and in Rainy River, routes eliminated and people having to travel considerable distances to pick up their mail. Indeed, I have seen lifetime customers taken off the delivery, people who had received their mail at a particular location in a box for decades no longer being able to get it there but having to travel to town, and in one case up to 70 kilometres on a round trip to pick up the mail.
May 26, 1987

These are not the only people who feel disenfranchised and left out because of Canada Post's efforts to reduce its deficits. Remote fly-in communities in my constituency, almost all Indian reserve communities, want to operate for themselves the local post offices which have been controlled for many years by companies such as the Hudson Bay Company which have their roots outside the community. This is something that the Post Office should look at now that the Hudson Bay Company has sold many of the stores which operate these post offices. Is it an appropriate time to look at a post office that is controlled by the community and where the economic benefits, the economic opportunity of operating the post office, in communities where there is very little in the way of economic benefit, can go to the permanent residents of the community?
In some communities delivery service is so erratic as to be appalling. It is a matter of pure conjecture and speculation as to whether the mail-bag will get off the plane on the day that it is supposed to get off the plane. The principle of fair and equal service that is mentioned in the Opposition Day motion is indeed a principle that in many communities in my riding is honoured more in the breach that in the observance.
For example, we have the case of communities that are totally unserved by Canada Post. These are communities where there is no mail delivery, communities such as Lac la Croix, Poplar Hill, Slate Falls, and MacDowell Lake. These are communities in which the only way of getting mail in is through the courtesy or generosity of a small airline, or even a private aircraft owner, who will pick up a bag of mail at the post office at his or her own expense of time and cost and bring it into the community on a sporadic basis, on the basis of when the opportunity to fly to the community occurs. That surely is not fair and equal service. There are other instances in which fair and equal service as a principle has been totally undermined.
In the case of a house in Fort Frances that stands on one corner of an intersection, the owner must go to the post office to pick up his mail while at the same time on the other three corners of that intersection the home owners benefit from door-to-door delivery. That is an example which I am sure we could furnish the details of to the Minister if the Minister cared to take an interest.
[Translation)
Faced with the Government's inaction on this issue, what are Canadians doing? Last December, Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of attending a major meeting in the small community of Esprit-Saint, near Rimouski. In this community of some 600 people from what I was told, there was a meeting of over 800 people. It was the largest audience, not including my party's conventions, I have ever addressed as guest speaker. The meeting was also attended by the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic (Mrs. Killens) whom I now see in the House. It was during that meeting that the group "Dignite rurale du Canada" was formed to convince the Government not to make the cuts suggested in the corporate plan of the Canada Post.
Supply
Mr. Gilles Raymond, from Esprit-Saint, was elected president of this organization, which is seeking a fair and equitable treatment for rural regions. It should be emphasized that this meeting had the support of representatives from other Canadian provinces, including Ontario, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, and British Columbia.
This organization, born in a Quebec village, now extends from coast to coast. For "Dignite rurale du Canada", the cuts contemplated in the plan threaten the very foundations of rural life in Canada.
As was noted by Mr. Raymond at a recent press conference, rural residents have the reputation of being stubborn and will never accept second class citizen treatment. And that is what is a stake in the Canada Post plan. Now that "Dignite rurale du Canada" includes representatives from all over this country, from all kinds of groups and organizations, from postal service users to postmasters and postal unions, it will speak with a booming voice throughout rural Canada, and we shall hear a lot from these people over the next few months.

I am happy not only to have been at the founding convention but to have seen the progress that Rural Dignity of Canada is making in bringing these important matters of postal service to the attention of the House of Commons and to the attention of the people of Canada.
Before I conclude I would like to turn briefly to some of the confrontational actions which are instanced in the opposition motion. We have had recruitment, the attempted recruitment of part-timers for a salary of $4.50 per hour on the understanding that they are to be willing to cross a picket line. We have had the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), whose rhetoric very rarely stays below the level of the inflammatory, say that maybe the military could deliver the post in the event of a strike-a great contribution, one must admit, to labour-management harmony.
O)
We have seen Canada Post stripped of representatives of labour on its board. While I do not say that Canada Post or the Government is entirely responsible for any confrontations which might occur-and I recognize that these things have a dynamic of their own-frankly we must acknowledge that the combative attitude of the Government and the obscurantist rhetoric which it allows some of its members to use cannot do anything but exacerbate the situation. Some of the roll-backs which have been demanded are obviously intended to provoke.
In today's edition of The Toronto Sun we have a report about security frisks which they are planning to introduce. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate on the motion put forward by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). It concerns the continued deterioration of Canada postal service by undermining the principle of fair and equal services to all Canadians through the substitution of "supermailboxes" for door-to-door service and by the closure of rural post offices.
I should like to stop there and emphasize "the closure of rural post offices". I will return to that particular aspect of the motion a little later.
The motion continues as follows: "by exacerbating already disintegrating labour-management relations within Canada Post by removing labour representation from the Corporation's Board and by other confrontational actions, thereby increasing the threats of postal service disruptions or even shut-downs".
Indeed the subject matter is an important one. I believe the contents of the opposition Motion adequately represent the concerns of many Canadians with regard to this particular subject matter.
It should be noted that there have been numerous discussions about this particular Crown corporation. We have had the minority report of the Standing Committee on Government Operations which examined the 1986-87 to 1990-91 Canada Post corporate plan. In examining the corporate plan it becomes obvious to many, but particularly to those of us who have the great privilege of representing small rural communities throughout Canada, that there is a desire and an intention on behalf of the Government of Canada to prejudice, even more so than it already has, the aspirations of Canadians who live in small, rural, remote communities.
In less than 15 years from now we will be in the year 2000. I think in recent years there has been a trend toward a greater concentration of Canadians in urban areas as opposed to rural communities. Notwithstanding that particular fact of Canadian life, it is important for those individuals and for Members of Parliament who represent urban constituencies to understand and appreciate rural Canadian life.
I should like to name a few of these communities in my constituency such as Donkin, South Bar, New Victoria, Gabarouse, Sydney Forks, East Bay, St. Peter's, Louisburg, Dominion, Glace Bay, and Waterford. It is true that they do not have a CN Tower. It is true that they do not have a dome. Hon. Members opposite laugh, but it is rural Canadian life.
One of its pillars has been the institution of post offices. I know that Tories have-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext: One every two and a half miles.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS

It is a meeting place for members of the community to visit with others, to exchange information, to obtain information, and of course to receive their mail. This may mean the winning of a particular grant or honorarium from Government, whether national or provincial. It may be a letter from a loved one out of the country. It may be a variety of communications. Nevertheless, they have played a very important part in Canadian life.
When I listen to Hon. Members opposite talk about the closure of post offices, I find it rather frustrating to hear them, with great fanfare and smiles on their faces, say that they can close post offices without concern for the people who live in those communities. Let it be said that the symbolism that that represents to Canadian rural life is extremely important. I would think Hon. Members opposite would not want to see Canadian symbolism vis-a-vis the auspices of our postal stations across the country deteriorate if they believe as I do- and I am certain they do-in terms of Canadian unity.
The question which rural communities ask Members of Parliament, the question with which I have been confronted as a Member of Parliament is a simple one. If we lose our post offices today, what will we lose tomorrow?

speechtext: The Liberals.

speechtext:

May 26, 1987

If we lose the Post Office, what do we lose next? That is the question, Mr. Speaker. The community I represent called Marion Bridge is made up of a cross-section of different individuals of different political persuasion, young and old, the unemployed and those who run small businesses who happen to live in that rural part of Cape Breton known as Marion Bridge. They were appalled to hear that the Government is contemplating closing their particular facility. They asked "What will we lose next?" Of course, the answer that government Members give is that that is not important, the ramifications, the linkages, are not important. I suggest that those ramifications are important. A rural post office whether in Summer-side, Prince Edward Island, Westmoreland-Kent, St. Leonard-a more urban area than mine-but wherever those post offices close, there are linkages. All Members of Parliament ought to be very concerned about that. Of course, the chairman of the Alberta Conservative caucus agrees with me, at least I am led to believe he does. In February, 1987 he is alleged to have said-I hope I am quoting his correctly because I would not want to steal the Hon. Member's thunder-"Canada Post discriminates. What are the consequences for small towns and villages as a result of the closure of the rural post office? The former Minister responsible for Canada Post, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) said, "In villages and small towns across Canada, the Post Office remains one of the most frequently visited places by citizens of the community. The Post Office has, over the years, become a much needed resource centre. Members of the community know where to go in order to obtain information on a variety of subjects. The federal Government is everywhere in Canada. The Post Office is still the most familiar place which brings information to people. speechtext:
The situation in which we find ourselves is that Canadians from differert walks of life have now stated their views on the importance of a Canada Post Corporation. I know on the other side of the coin there are problems in Canada Post. We know of the delays, if you will, in delivering the mail. We realize that the deficit of that Corporation is a concern to all Canadians. I think we also realize that that particular Crown corporation, when you compare it with others, is not as bad a performer as some government Members would lead us to believe. For instance, what was Canada Post created for? To gather and distribute mail, not to make profits for the federal Government as we know is the case with provincial liquor control boards and lottery commissions. That is not to suggest that governments, regardless of their political persuasion should not attempt to try to balance the cost and revenues. Should the citizens who I happen to represent in rural parts of my constituency always be the victims of such government cut-backs? Why can it not be other areas of government activity if that is the way the Government wishes to proceed?
Given the size of the operating budget, Canada Post is probably the public service which costs the Government the smallest amount of money, having given Canada Post only $184 milion in fiscal 1985-86 or 6.2 per cent of the Corporation's total budget. The Government has to recognize that no other Crown corporation of comparable size-60,000 employees-has in modern history achieved a comparable performance. I make that statement, not suggesting that the Government is entirely wrong for trying to balance the books. But I think it has to be said, Mr. Speaker, that there are a number of Crown corporations which do not perform as adequately as Canada Post. For the sake of comparison, one could look at the performance of other Crown corporations such as CN or CBC. Our Public Broadcasting Corporation has an operating budget of $1.1 billion. The public purse contributes $881 million to that particular Crown corporation. The rest of the money is raised through advertising contracts let out by the Corporation.

May 26, 1987
Supply
One can argue, and argue effectively, that perhaps the goals and aspirations of the CBC, as opposed to the goals and aspirations of Canada Post, are different. They are serving different purposes, et cetera. I wish to make the point for for Members on both sides that when you look at the effectiveness of this Crown corporation it has not been as bad as Members opposite would lead us to believe.
In the case of Canada Post Corporation, the Government has never had to finance more than 12 per cent of the organization's budget since it became a Crown corporation on October 16, 1981. In fact, the federal contribution went from 10.3 per cent in 1982-83 to 6.2 per cent in 1985-86. There were increases in the federal contribution until the fiscal year 1984-85, the famous 12 per cent indicated earlier, and then the decrease with which we are now familiar.
That is the corporate side. In the several minutes I have remaining, I would like to touch on the human side of Canada Post. I talked about the importance of rural post offices to this country. I say very sincerely that they are important to the economic life in various communities. What is also important is the human aspect of post office closures and what those closures are doing to labour relations and morale in the post offices.
I have spoken to a number of union members who work at post offices in some of the major and not so major centres. I have not found a great desire on their part to go out on strike. Rather, I found that they have a desire to raise their families and to have job security. I do not find anything inherently wrong with that, but, as my colleague has pointed out as well, I do see signs of a Government that seems to want to seek out a confrontation with Canada Post. I hope that is not the case. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader is shaking his head. I do not know if he is saying yes or no.

speechtext: Not the case.
