speechtext:
He said it is not the case. I hope that is so.
We must remember that if there is a confrontation, the management of the corporation must assume its responsibility because it is a function of management that it set the example for the rank and file to follow.
I say to the Government that it is wrong to close rural post offices across Canada because of their importance to rural Canadian life. I would hope that the Government would curtail this confrontational attitude which seems to have besieged Canada Post Corporation and which I believe is affecting negatively the esprit de corps within the corporation as well as the effectiveness of the delivery of mail.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the question of rural mail delivery and post offices, two assurances have been given by the Minister responsible. First, he has assured us that no rural routes will be cut, but because of the organized attempt at
scare tactics in much of this debate and in media discussion, that message is not getting through. Second, the Minister has made it clear that post offices in rural Canada will not be closed in an arbitrary manner. In cases of attrition, a post office might be re-evaluated with a view to improving the service to the people in the area. That in a nutshell is very much the position as 1 understand it put forward by the Minister on the important question of postal service.
What is reprehensible is that there have been organized attempts by special interest groups to instil in the Canadian public a fear that postal services will be cut off, that rural routes will be cut off any day and that post offices will be closed any day. The people fear that they will simply wake up some morning and there will be no mail delivery. Of course, that is far from the truth. It is a product of the imagination of special interest groups and serves no constructive purpose.
Canadians who are genuinely interested in mail service and in ensuring the continued high level of mail service deserve to know the facts. They deserve to be treated in an honest manner by all groups interested in participating in the debate on Canada's postal service.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has made some comments that are worth exploring a little further. Quite frankly, if one could accept the Hon. Member's thesis in its entirety, one would then logically say that perhaps the rural post offices that have been closed will be reinstated. Second, one would ask who has caused this fear. He has indicated that it has been special interest groups.
Let us look at special interest groups. Say, perhaps, a letter carrier, an individual who runs a very small post office in a community or a contractor who delivers mail sees rural post offices being closed. Is there anything inherently wrong with those who may be affected or are likely to be affected seeking out others who may share a similar view and a similar purpose? Is there anything wrong with them coming together to discuss the importance of a particular rural post office and the delivery of the mail? I do not find anything inherently wrong with those sorts of interest groups.
Representatives of many interest groups have come to see me. Perhaps some of them were of different political persuasions, but nevertheless, they were concerned about the importance of rural post offices to their communities. I do not fault them one bit for that and I do not think Members of Parliament would want to fault them for it either intentionally or unintentionally.
In conclusion, it is nice to hear members of the Government say that members of the Opposition are only using fear tactics. If that were the case, I do not think union representatives, municipal leaders and farm federations would be demanding that the Government change the provisions of its corporate plan or, more recently, change some of the actions it has taken.
Rural post offices are very important. I believe that because of the fight members of the Opposition have put up over the last number of weeks and months, we have given this issue
May 26, 1987

such a high profile that we have been able to force the Government to back-track on some of its decisions. I hope that will carry on into the weeks and months ahead as we progress into a new session of Parliament or indeed our next Government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is full of poppycock, the whole can. He knows full well that he did not have anything to do with turning around the management plan of Canada Post. Not for long. You guys are seeing to that.
While the Hon. Member has this holier than thou attitude let us just for a moment assess the people of that particular community. who have written to me regarding that. They are fearful not because of what the Opposition or the media has said. They are fearful because of the Government's actions to date in closing post offices and the effect this is having on their lives.
The Hon. Member ought to come clean and tell it like it is. The Government is trying to close down rural post offices in those constituencies represented by Liberal and NDP Members of Parliament. That is what you are trying to do.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate this opportunity to enter the debate. I have listened with great interest to my hon. friend who just spoke. When we challenged him to name one post office closed by our Government he was unable to do so.
The motion condemns the Government for allowing deterioration of the postal service. It cites a host of misleading statements about postal service and management relations. I think it became very evident as the debate progressed that Hon. Members opposite have completely failed to prove their case, and I am pleased to have this opportunity to set the record straight. The House will know that the Liberal Party was the Government of the day when the majority of Canada Post problems really began. The Post Office came out of the 1960s and 1970s with a host of challenges. Its reputation for maintaining anything resembling a regular service was damaged by recurring strikes resulting from the Liberal Party's inability to handle labour negotiations. The rate of absenteeism was allowed by the Liberal Party during that time to go up to double the norm. The situation became more complex because the Liberals allowed the bargaining unit to be divided into some 30 separate parts. Settlements were costly and eroded the fundamental rights of management that were needed. That is why our Party argued for a Crown corporation to deliver the mail, and when the previous Government saw the light and brought in the Canada Post Act, our Party supported it. However, that did not mean we could cure the problems of the Post Office immediately.
First we had the 6 and 5 program of the Liberal Party. That put a halt to negotiations with the postal unions during the early part of the corporation's mandate. Two years passed without any meaningful bargaining between the parties. Under our Government there has been one agreement reached with all the bargaining units covering some 48,000 employees. That was the longest period of labour stability in the Post Office since 1968 when the unions were given the right to collective bargaining.
The opposition Parties are trying to suggest that there is going to be a postal strike. It is unfortunate, as was suggested earlier, that they are using scare tactics by saying we intend to force a strike. We are negotiating in good faith and progress has been made. Yet we realize there is a need for fundamental

May 26, 1987
Supply
changes in the contract to deal with such issues as productivity, the efficient use of manpower and equipment, reduction of absenteeism, flexibility in operations, and a move towards competitive wage levels.
One thing we are trying to do, as opposed to the previous Government, is to focus the negotiations at the table and take them away from the media and the political arena. Under our Government the negotiations are being conducted by seasoned negotiators. The issue is not being politicized because, as far as we are concerned, it is an operational question, not a political question. We believe it is in the best interests of Canadians to let the Canada Post management and the unions negotiate their collective agreements with each other without political interference. Working together will bring about a reasonable settlement and a respectable and viable postal service. We believe the parties themselves can best set those parameters. We feel confident the Parties can reach a fair, effective and equitable collective agreement. We know that our side is bargaining in good faith and we feel that is happening on the other side, too.
I want to talk now for a minute about what Canada Post is supposed to be providing to Canadians, that is, a reliable, efficient and predictable postal service which will enable Canadians to receive properly prepared mail at a reasonable cost. We do not say that we will be doing it in exactly the same way as it has been done in the past. This is a big and sparsely populated country. The services vary according to the population density and the local conditions. For example, a downtown area may have the density to justify door-to-door delivery of mail by letter carrier. There is just not the density to justify the same service in smaller towns or rural areas. This does not mean that the people living there are second-class citizens. It means that the commitment to deliver the mail is met in different ways.
I represent the Town of Penetanguishene of 5,000 people, all of whom go to the post office to get their mail. They did so under the Liberals and are doing so under the Conservatives. That is no great hardship. There is, however, some criticism to be made of the previous Liberal administration because the post office is at the bottom of the hill. However, they go to get their mail.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we will continue to have a variety of ways of delivering the mail. To my colleagues from the big city who expect everything handed to them on a platter I say that that is too bad. In Penetanguishene they go to the post office and pick up their mail. We live in an era in which people are more mobile. The convenience store is the norm. I do not have any difficulty with people going somewhere to get their mail.
1 want to talk for a minute about the supermailbox. Canada Post introduced the supermailbox to allow customers to receive mail and also to send it. It is suggested, and I agree, that the supermailbox is a big improvement over the green group mailboxes. When we say that we are going to eliminate the ugly green boxes over the next three years and replace them with the supermailbox, I am sure we will have the support of everybody in this House. I see my colleague, the critic for the NDP, smiling and nodding agreement. I am pleased to have his support on that. The corporation adds some 130,000 addresses each year as new homes and businesses are created. This is the best way of dealing with the problem. That is why Canada Post is developing new concepts and community mail centres.
I want to read to you, Mr. Speaker, a letter which will be circulated to all Members of Parliament. It is dated May 15, 1987, and I have just had it translated. It is addressed to the Hon. Harvie Andre, Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It says:
Dear Harvie:
Please record me as a strong supporter of Canada Post's super mail box program. I am completely opposed to any further increases in the price of stamps to provide universal door-to-door mail delivery. That money can be better spent on social programs or tax reductions.
In my opinion super mail boxes should be provided, everywhere there is not door-to-door delivery, immediately! All green group boxes should be replaced immediately! They are a disgrace!
In this day and age door-to-door delivery is as inefficient and impractical as door-to-door delivery of bread and milk. This is a day and age when more and more people are out of their homes each day. They pass by potential super mail box locations regularly. In fact, many of my constituents have never had door-to-door delivery. It is an unnecessary luxury, not an essential service.
Therefore, count me as a super mail box supporter. In addition, when all the super mail boxes are installed for those who presently do not have any service, please write me another letter and I will support a complete conversion to super mail boxes for everyone.
That is where I stand on the question of supermailboxes.
I want to talk about some other things with regard to our present mail system.

speechtext: The material I have is very important and, as you can see, I am driven to speak.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA POST-POSTAL SERVICE- LABOUR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS
speechtext:
I want to talk about the present postal system. We believe that it does not meet the needs of the public. The post offices were built long ago to meet the demographic patterns of the day, those of another era. That is why in many cases the post office is not located where people do the rest of their shopping. There is no place to park and it is not open at the same convenient hours as stores.
We believe that Canada Post should use the convenience and expertise of private retail businesses to make its services and products more available to Canadians. Under the administration of the Liberal Party you could buy postage stamps only at the post office. Through franchising we will make it as easy for Canadians to buy stamps as it is to buy cigarettes and lottery tickets. I do not know why the NDP does not support that concept of supplying a service to Canadians.
May 26, 1987

My hon. colleague shakes his head when I suggest that we will make it easy for Canadians to buy stamps. Why not? What is the matter with the storeowner who sells a lottery ticket also selling a stamp? What is the big mystery about stamps? Why can Canadians not buy them anywhere they want? The New Democratic Party does not want people to be able to buy stamps anywhere.
Let it be shown on the record that the Conservative Party wants to make it easy for Canadians to buy stamps. We believe it is a commodity which one should be able to purchase anywhere. That is the reason behind our policy for franchising Post Office operations. We want to make it easy to buy stamps, register letters and send parcels. It is a tragedy that the NDP is against this.
There has been some suggestion that we are amalgamating post offices and eliminating obvious redundancies. That is not a new matter. It has happened in the past and will happen in the future. We want to make the system more efficient. In the future we will not be building buildings and hiring people to provide access. We will instead use the modern tool of today, the supermailbox. We will consult with people when we amalgamate post offices, as my hon. colleague suggested. We are committed to a reliable service. We are committed to delivering the mail.
The vast majority of the mail is delivered on time. However, the percentage of failures spread over the number of people affected can certainly make it look as though there were some problems. We admit that this service is not as reliable as we want it to be and was not as reliable as we wanted it to be in the past. Our administration is reviewing the system and procedures.

NATIONAL REVENUE-ADMINISTRATION OF FARM FUEL TAX REBATE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I directed a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) on April 7, 1987, regarding the administration of the farm fuel tax rebate. At that time the Minister of National Revenue assured the House that he and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had been discussing the possibility of improvement to the administrative efficiency of the program. He sought ways in which the program could be made even more beneficial.
The program is already very beneficial to the producers. It is not, however, particularly beneficial to the many bulk fuel dealers who are forced to carry the delivery costs of this program. The farm fuel tax relief program reduces the burden of farm input costs. It is one of the ways by which the Government is helping Canadian farmers fight the cost price squeeze. The rebates on farm gasoline and diesel fuel effectively offset the federal sales and excise tax on these products. These rebates have saved Canadian farmers more than $100 million in 1986-87.
The problem with the farm fuel tax relief program is not with the treatment of the consumer, but with the application of the program to bulk fuel dealers. There are essentially two kinds of bulk fuel dealers. There is the commission agent who holds his inventory on consignment. Thus, the inventory he holds is free of any sales tax. There is the independent who purchases his fuel from a manufacturer and pays sales tax on the purchased fuel. His inventory is tax paid.
All dealers can sell fuel to the primary producers free of tax. However, the crux of the matter is that the independent bulk fuel dealers have to apply to the federal Government to secure a refund of the sales tax which they have already paid on their inventory at the time of purchase from the refiner. The independent has to secure a refund, but the commission agent does not. In other words, the independent bulk fuel dealer must carry some of the Government's cost of delivering this program while the commission agent does not have to do so.
What is the cost to the independent dealer? It is the interest foregone for various periods on almost $29 million in tax rebates between December 1, 1984 and December 31, 1986. It should be noted that the independent dealer has no choice but to claim rebates on behalf of their customers. While this is an elective provision of the program in theory, the real world gives the independent fuel dealer no other choice. If he does not collect the rebate on behalf of his customer, he loses the customer.
It is worth noting that any delay between the time of sale by the independent bulk fuel dealer to his customers and the time he actually receives reimbursement of that tax upon application to the federal Government is an inappropriate cost to the dealer to deliver the federal Government program. Furthermore, any delay puts the independent dealer at a competitive disadvantage to the commission agent. In other words, the Government program, which should treat all dealers the same

May 26, 1987
Adjournment Debate
way, in fact treats one group more favourably than the other. I remind the House that most dealers are one person or at least one family operations.
I endorse the recommendation of over a year ago of either a provision for a cash advance or a float to dealers; or the payment of interest to dealers on the tax rebate owing by the Government.
It is worth noting that the turnaround time on refunds has improved from the 60 days that it was at the beginning of the program to about 40 days, as I am told by dealers. Elowever, I am told by bulk fuel dealers that they often have to apply for the current month's refund when they have not as yet received the previous month's refund. I submit that this is too much of a cost for those independent bulk fuel dealers to bear.

AIRPORTS-PROVISION OF FIRE-FIGHTING SERVICES- DEPARTMENT'S REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening my question on the Adjournment Debate is related to a matter of grave concern to many people. First, it concerns the travelling public.
My question relates to safety and the way in which our firefighters and those who work to deal with crashes of aircraft cope with emergencies at our airports. My question tonight relates to the way in which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has evaded his responsibilities in dealing with the protection of the public when it travels in aircraft and the protection of flight crews which have the responsibility to fly aircraft into our airports-in fact, it relates to the safety of all concerned.
The Minister was asked by myself on March 31 about this matter. At that time I brought to his attention the fact that the Government is trying to save a measly $1 million by cutting back from seven to five the required number of people who should be on hand to carry out fire-fighting, safety and crash emergency work.
A further point I made was that the number of personnel hours has actually been reduced and that, in fact, some of our airports have acted at times, from midnight until 8 a.m. on one occasion in the case of Regina airport, with no fire-fighters at all at the site while very large planes arrived. This lack of concern about the well-being of the public is absolutely scandalous.
[DOT]	(1810)
I should like to ask again the question which the Minister evaded. Why is he trying to save $1 million by cutting back on safety? In fact the Canadian Association of Airline Pilots brought to his attention that they do not even feel safe in landing airplanes in Canadian airports in light of the developments resulting from a change in air transport safety policy by the Minister. He has cut back the number of dollars available to bring in people when crews are short staffed because of illness or whatever. There is no money to bring in people under those circumstances.
We also see that the handicapped are gravely endangered by the new policy. We hear pious words from the Government about its concern in the area of transportation for the handicapped. In fact, some dollars have been put into the effort. On the other hand, they have been nullified and the lives of the handicapped are endangered.
The minimum number of people required to put out a fire is five people with five trucks. We know perfectly well that four
May 26, 1987

trucks and one person being used to direct is not adequate. The job of fire-fighters is not only to put out the fire or to make a passageway so that people can escape from the airplane. We also know that they have an obligation to go on board the airplane if necessary to save passengers. For example, if the crew inside is overcome, it is the task of fire-fighters to save the people on board. We know perfectly well that four trucks with four drivers and one person directing is an impossible situation.
Contrary to what the Minister tried to lead us to believe, the task is not merely to clear a passageway. One primary task of fire-fighters is to go aboard airplanes to save lives. We certainly know that handicapped people need extra help. Also we know that the trucks have rescue equipment with which to save people, not merely put out fires. The purpose of rescue squads is to save lives. One would in fact think that it would be the primary concern.
The reply of the Minister of Transport was totally inadequate. In fact, he played with words in order to confuse us rather than be forthcoming about the fact that his changes in the regulations have greatly endangered the public, the people who are flying airplanes, and in fact fire-fighters themselves, by reducing their ability to call in people when someone has reported sick to bring their staff up to full strength or to call in people to fill in for other part-time workers.
About half the time we find airports manned by the minimum number according to the statistics given by CALPA. Sometimes they do not even have the required number because of problems such as illness or other reasons.
I would suggest that the Minister was playing with words when he suggested that there was no reduction in staff because there are 657 full-time employees. However, all provisions for on-call staff are obliterated. Most airports work with a minimum number now. Therefore, with no on-call staff available, there is in fact a reduction in staff.
This morning Transport Canada staged a mock airport disaster at Pearson International Airport. Thousands of dollars were spent on videos to show how a disaster would be taken care of. First, there were some hitches. Second, and contrary to what the Minister of Transport said, what actually happened was that the Mississauga fire-fighters were at the airport standing by, on hand, whereas in reality it takes from 15 minutes to half an hour for auxiliary fire-fighters from Mississauga to reach the Pearson International Airport. It was a fraud, and the Minister of Transport should own up to it.

subtopic: CITIZENSHIP COURTS-DELAY IN PROCESSING APPLICATIONS- APPOINTMENT OF JUDGES
CITIZENSHIP COURTS-DELAY IN PROCESSING APPLICATIONS- APPOINTMENT OF JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 4 of this year I asked the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie) the following question:
Is the Minister aware that thousands of people in such cities as Calgary await processing of their citizenship applications, meanwhile having lost the right to travel using the passports of their countries of origin?
The Secretary of State of Canada replied:
yes, 1 am aware of the problem. We are trying to address it with existing resources.
I then followed with the question:
How soon does the Minister expect to appoint enough citizenship judges to ensure that people will not be kept waiting months to receive Canadian citizenship during this fortieth anniversary of the Citizenship Act?
To that question, the Secretary of State responded:
the report from Dr. Sutherland is now available. In fact, I received it on Friday afternoon. I hope to make appointments by mid-May.
The matter of having enough citizenship court judges to ensure that persons who wish to become Canadian citizens can do so expeditiously is an important matter to every person involved in the process. As I suggested in one of my questions, it involves the specific hardship faced by those persons who have applied for Canadian citizenship and have to wait many months, living in uncertainty because they have lost their right to travel on the passports of the countries from which they came. If anything were to require their return, if compassionate circumstances were to arise, they might find themselves in very real difficulty. That human aspect of the situation calls on the Government to deal expeditiously with this matter.
I would like to suggest that the problem that has arisen is symptomatic of other difficulties the Government has created and that the failure in this area is typical of the slowness of action in other areas, such as the revision of the Official Languages Act and the presentation of amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act which have been promised for many, many months and for which we continue to wait. It is symptomatic of the failure of the Department headed by Captain Canada, as he himself likes to be called when speaking to students, to focus on the shortcomings in the appointments of Citizenship Court judges by the Secretary of State. I say this with all the more energy because this is after all the fortieth anniversary of the Citizenship Act.
Citizenship Courts themselves are an essential experience for those who want to become Canadians. It should be a good experience. Yet, because of the delays that have arisen for some who will soon be fellow citizens, they are experiencing just the opposite of the kind of good government they should experience. This experience of inefficiency was forcefully presented to me in Calgary where 4,000 persons have applied and some have waited for as long as eight months. This really underscores the urgency of this matter.
I do not suppose all of these potential Canadians realize that the problem has to do with the patronage system which prevails in the Canadian Government. They do not realize that in the past months, the persons who were appointed by the previous Government have come to the end of their terms and this Government, through the well established system of patronage that exists, has allowed appointments to lapse without acting expeditiously to appoint new persons. This, of course, leaves us wondering about the patronage system which operates through the Prime Minister's Office and the Cabinet. This is, in fact, a little lesson in the nuts and bolts of the Canadian political system that is being experienced by these soon to be fellow citizens.
Since the last weeks of 1986, there has been a further difficulty in that some of the persons who had been appointed, and specifically two judges, came into controversy because of the kinds of questions they asked and the kinds of conversations they carried on with applicants for Canadian citizenship.
I recognize that that has probably complicated things for Captain Canada and, I suppose, has justified some investigation of the situation.
Clearly, the process of examining applicants for Canadian citizenship should be carried out in a careful, impartial and dispassionate manner. I always appreciate the opportunity to take part in Citizenship Courts in Thunder Bay. In this way they present Canadian life and Canadian Government in the best possible way.
I want to note that the Secretary of State of Canada was quoted last month in The Globe and Mail as saying that good government makes good politics. All we have to do is practice good government. I could not agree more. Applicants for Canadian citizenship are waiting for just that kind of demonstration. We have not had any judges appointed since the middle of May. In fact, there has been only one renewal and one new appointment over the last five months.
May 26, 1987

If I were to provide some further advice to the Minister concerning Citizenship Court judges, I would commend to him a phrase he himself used, something that was said by one of our Fathers of Confederation, Thomas Darcy McGee. He said more than 100 years ago that we should lift ourselves to the level of our destinies, rise above all low limitations and narrow circumscriptions, cultivate that true catholicity of spirit which embraces all creeds, all classes and all races, in order to make of our boundless province, so rich in known and unknown resources, a great new northern nation. That is the spirit in which Citizenship Court judges should be acting, and I trust that the Minister will shortly be appointing judges who can fulfil their functions in just that spirit.

The purpose of all this is to update our Citizenship Act and strenghten it to emphasize the rights as well as the challenges attached to our status as Canadian citizens.

Adjournment Debate
which implies that we have also had to review the citizenship judge appointment process.

speechtext:
Order, please.
Mr. President, on behalf of all Members of the Senate and the House of Commons, we welcome you to the Parliament of Canada.
We are honoured to have you in our midst.

I now invite the Right Honourable the Prime Minister to introduce our distinguished guest.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. President, it is a profoundly moving occasion for me to introduce you to the Members of our House of Commons and Senate. Your presence in this Chamber marks a highpoint in relations between our two countries.
The visit you embark upon today is without doubt inspired by friendship. Yet we know it must be viewed equally in a broader context, one that embraces both continuity and change.
Your purpose in coming here was to affirm the enduring ties that bind us: language and culture, our allegiance to the values of freedom and democracy, and the solidarity that has drawn us closer in times of crisis.
From the trenches of Picardy in one war, to the beaches of Normandy in the next, thousands of Canadians have made the ultimate sacrifice for liberty.
As they are remembered in the hearts of their fellow citizens in Canada, so is their memory honoured in France, from Vimy Ridge to Beny-sur-Mer. One is a famed memorial, and the other a simple country cemetery where French and Englishspeaking Canadians, officers and enlisted men, without
distinction as to language or rank, have found a final resting place together.
Nowhere is our nation more united, Mr. President, that in such small corners of yours. In rendering homage at our National Cenotaph this morning, you have not only honoured all Canadians, but also the memory of those brave souls.
The durability of France, the constancy and creativity she represents, are personified today in one of her most distinguished sons, a great President who has our respect and admiration and whom we welcome.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ADDRESS
speechtext:
Yet at the same time, your official visit comes amid the irreversible tide that sweeps all shores and demands a new perspective.

Our country has taken decisive steps in the course of an intensive but necessary evolution which has made us more aware of our own identity.
We have summoned the national resolve and the clarity of purpose to face the vital challenges of our time. We resolved them in our own country, among ourselves, as we should, in the full exercise of our sovereignty. In so doing, we have found the way to a new national consensus. Today, Canada is following that path with determination, fully aware of our responsibility toward the future.
Twenty years after General de Gaulle's visit, you will find, Mr. President, a Canada at peace with itself, aware of its diversity and resolved to recognize it with respect, tolerance and generosity. In the week ahead you will cross a country that spans a continent, a nation confident of its role and eager to contribute its share to world peace and justice.
For the first time a President of the French Republic will officially travel across Canada to the heartland of the Prairies and then on to a great metropolitan area in Toronto. For the first time he will bear France's greetings to Canadians of Acadian descent after renewing the special cordial ties between his country and Quebec.
Today we turn a new page in the history of the relationship between France and Canada. We cannot change the past, but we can shape our future. What matters is the chapter we write together. It holds great promise for political rapprochement, industrial co-operation and increased trade.
Mr. President, on behalf of all Canadians may I tell you that your presence here today will contribute enormously to the renewal of that relationship.
[ Translation]
Another way to fulfil these hopes is by achieving francophone solidarity. History will credit you as the artisan of the Paris Summit, where heads of state and government from some 40 countries, and all five continents, gathered last year.
May 26, 1987

The agreement we reached with the Governments of Quebec and New Brunswick, as you know, removed the final obstacle to building a new solidarity within the French-speaking community. The Government of Canada eagerly joined this worthy venture.
The interests of Canada as a whole, embracing both French and English cultures, demand that we foster our participation in La Francophonie and the Commonwealth. This double window on the world makes Canada the meeting-place of two of the great currents of international relations.
As a manifestation of our commitment to La Francophonie, it was our desire that Quebec City be the site of the second Summit this coming September. Let no one overlook the significance of holding the Summit on the banks of the St. Lawrence. It is a clear and serene recognition of Canada's, and Quebec's, role in the francophone family.
We desire to fulfil this vocation as equals, following an approach focused on modern and concrete objectives.
Other, equally pressing considerations, warrant and require closer ties with France.
These stem from Europe's importance in international politics and economics. As an inexhaustible reservoir of human resources and skills, and as an enlarged community, Europe plays a pre-eminent role in world affairs.
Flow could anyone overlook the unified domestic market of 320 million consumers the Europe of the 90s will become? And how could anyone not see that France lies at the very heart of the grand design of Europe?

That is another reason why we are working to develop even closer ties with your country.
But our co-operation must be nourished with substance, and must develop around initiatives that touch the basic interests of our two nations. We must expand the scope of our bilateral activities, involving scientists, for example, and business leaders. Above all, we must never relent in the persistence of our efforts. For we are only at the beginning of the road, which is as long as the successes awaiting us can be far-reaching.
And there shall be problems, perhaps some serious problems, along the way. The issue of fishing quotas and the fixing of the boundary line for the offshore limits around St. Pierre and Miquelon constitute a test of our political maturity and ability to resolve our differences through the promotion of our mutual interests. France must surely be aware of the difficult nature of this controversy, and of the seriousness of the issues it raises for our fishermen in Atlantic Canada, as well as for Canadian sovereignty. 1 know, Mr. President, you share my view that this matter be resolved fairly.

Your stay among us comes at a moment in history when the dynamics of the situation and our own aims have converged. We have before us a wide field of responsibilities. We have before us opportunities which history, and our own peoples, will not permit to slip away.
The time has come not only for awareness, but for action; not only to renew promises, but to fulfil them; not only to evoke our roots, but to make them bear fruit.
We Canadians cherish our unique heritage from France, her elan, her culture, her humanism. We cherish her as one of our two mother countries.
Loyal as they are to the values of the past, we are also mindful of the realities of tomorrow. That is why Canadians choose to go forward together, with you, with France.
Mr. President, I speak on behalf of all Canadians in saying how happy and delighted we are to have you among us.
All week long, Mrs. Mitterrand and you will receive the special welcome we reserve for our fondest friend. At every stop, you will be reminded that Canada is, for France, a land of friendship and brotherhood.
Members of the House, distinguished Senators, I am honoured to present to you the President of the French Republic, Mr. Franqois Mitterrand.

speechtext:
Speakers of the House and the Senate, Prime Minister, ladies and gentlemen. 1 am moved by the tribute I have just received on behalf of France and 1 am honoured by this most cordial welcome to your Parliament.
After meeting this morning with Her Excellency the Governor General and with the Prime Minister, 1 now have the privilege of speaking to you, ladies and gentlemen, the elected representatives of Canada and guardians of the institutions that have made your country one of great democracies of the world.
Actually, 1 was a parliamentarian in my country for 35 years, in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. Since 1981, however, when I was elected President of the Republic, 1 have had to leave all that behind me. 1 do not have the right to enter the very precincts where I worked for so many years and where, in fact, 1 seldom received such a unanimous welcome. Sometimes there are feelings of regret, and when visiting one of our friends, as I am doing today, 1 like to compensate. I take a personal pleasure, as well as pride, in representing my country before assemblies like yours, and 1 want to thank you once again.
Perhaps I may comment, first of all, that Canada's political structures, that your country's economic and social framework and the positions you defend at the international level, reflect a focus on common ideals.

May 26, 1987
France and Canada share the conviction that they cannot conceive of a future without pluralism, without alternating majorities, the unrestricted expression of divergent views, and the rule of a majority that respects minorities.
On behalf of the French people, I would like to transmit to you, and through you to every man, woman and child in this country, the feelings of friendship of our country for yours. The message that France sends you is one of friendship and solidarity. And I could repeat, word for word, what was said by the Prime Minister, and I thank him for saying them. Because of the kind of society we have chosen, and notwithstanding differences that are grounded in our respective history, geography and customs, dialogue is second nature to us.
Indeed, our past has made the relationship between Canada and France a rather special one. Since the beginning of modern history and the time of the great explorers, the French have played a major role in the life of your country. The descendants of those who came here originally, who today number several million, represent over one quarter of the population and occupy a unique and inimitable position alongside their English-speaking compatriots. We see communities that are dynamic and enterprising, faithful to their traditions but also very much of this modern day and age and this continent. Unique and, at the same time, universal, they contribute to the rich diversity of this great country of yours. Canada's bicultural dimension brings joy to the heart of every Frenchman, and to my own, I can assure you, and perhaps I may also say a few words, although there would be so much to say, about the sacrifices made by your fathers and brothers in two World Wars. Whatever their origins and wherever they had their homes, whatever opposing sides they may have taken in the past, they were now fighting on the same side, with us. Would victory and freedom have been possible without the presence of these young men from all over the world, and particularly from Canada?
Prime Minister, you mentioned several historic places where the memory, suffering and death of so many are mourned, and where tragedy is still present in the hearts of so many mourners. It was the price we had to pay for freedom.
Ladies and gentlemen, we owe so much to your soldiers, and I would like to take this opportunity, at this solemn moment, to address these words to your compatriots who are listening to us now.
If I may, I would like to comment on some of the major issues of the day. My choice will be rather arbitrary, because otherwise there would be too much to say, and too little time to say it.
The world is in a crisis. Some people would say it always is. In any case, we have the feeling that the crisis we are experiencing today may be worse than at other times in our
history. Our problems are similar. We have to fight unemployment. We have to create a new environment to create new jobs and to prepare our countries for the next century. We must intensify all forms of intellectual creativity, we must intensify research and increase the capabilities of our intellects from childhood onward, so that we will finally have the means to master the secrets of the material world and thus enhance the human condition. We have to modernize our production equipment. We have to make our economies more competitive, since we are largely dependant on external trade. We have every interest in further developing trade between our countries. One imagines that Canada's natural tendency would probably be to trade mainly with the United States of America, while ours would be to trade with our Common Market neighbours. Nevertheless, I think that considering the modest level of our trade relationship, our two countries could do far more and far better. I hope that during this visit, we will be able to explore some possibilities for the future.
In fact, various agreements concluded in recent years have provided for increased co-operation in space, oceanology, oceanography and biotechnology, all of which involve new procedures that will stimulate industrial innovation. In January, we agreed to facilitate relations between our small business groups. Although relations between our scientists, industrialists and business people are little developed, there has been definite progress, both bilaterally-I am thinking of the SPOT satellite-and in connection with multilateral projects, and I refer to the European Eureka project. When our interests clash, on occasion, as on the fisheries issue, I believe that with a little common sense, concern for the law and the political will to settle disputes, we should be able to resolve these problems.
Ladies and gentlemen, at this point I would like to comment briefly on the world economic situation. The problems have been identified, and a response is of the essence. Prime Minister, in two weeks or so, we will be meeting again in Venice, where we shall have to deal with some of the problems that are of international concern.
I want to stress the urgency of some of the decisions to be made, and on an occasion that would seem entirely appropriate for discussing, in full recognition of the sovereignty and equality of our respective countries, the major problems we share, I would like to take this opportunity to outline four principles.
The first of these directions would be for countries with a trade surplus to use whatever leeway they have to boost their own growth and stimulate the growth of other countries.
The second direction would be to promote the recovery of the international monetary system by taking steps to stabilize exchange rates with respect to mutually agreed reference zones, to lower interest rates and to better co-ordinate efforts to control market speculation.
Thirdly, we should try to remove protectionist barriers in every area, since protectionism is present everywhere, in the
May 26, 1987

services, industrial and agricultural sectors. I know that discussions are under way with your neighbour, the United States of America, a special free trade agreement within the framework of GATT and along common rules. I wish you the best of success, granted that we have accepted common rules that apply to you as to ourselves. However, let us be open on this. Let us quit fighting over deadlocks between Europe and the American continent or Third World countries. Let us admit that protectionism is found in each and every country, and that what may be left for us to do is to compare and identify where protectionism is openly allowed in legislation or regulation, where it hides in hypocritical fashion behind the customs and traditions, where it takes the form of imperialist action, or simply where it so often appears by way of laisser-faire when leaders responsible for managing the world should in fact strive to reach an agreement for the well-being of all nations.
I have mentioned those three directions, but what I have is foremost in my mind at the present time is the fourth one. It is a concern with the future of the Third World, of developing countries, and especially with the problem of indebtedness. One may consider postponing the date of payment, extending repayment schedules for the most indebted countries. One could think of designing more generous procedures in the Club of Paris. But in my opinion, at the present time, we should mostly consider, without excluding any other solution, recycling on a multilateral basis part of the financial surpluses of those countries which do have surpluses. We should think of Japan, we might after all think of Germany too. Whoever reaches that stage, enjoys a fairly prosperous economy, should become very clearly aware of a new stage of responsibility. We would then increase the means of the international monetary fund. We would increase the capital of the World Bank and help those countries of the Third World which are among the poorest get through this tragedy which will eventually hurt the whole world.
I frequently tell my fellow citizens that there are probably two major war threats for the next century: The atomic bomb or nuclear war with unending confrontations leading to a competition that may reach a paroxysmal stage, but also the widening of the gap between rich and poor countries. Both our countries, though, are among the few which have decided to assign a significant percentage of their national product to the co-operation with the least developed countries.
I am aware of the increasing share of the Canadian revenue which is set aside every year throughout the world, through private initiatives or through the actions of public agencies, to fight under-development, and I thank you for that. I thank you, for that cause has been a deep, longstanding concern of mine.
As for France, it has significantly increased its assistance, especially in the past six years, and is intending to reach as
quickly as possible, as recommended by international institutions, the figure of .7 per cent of its Gross National Product to be used for development assistance.
But what is the reality we are facing today? Southern countries or so-called southern countries are hurt more than others by the slowing down of international growth, by the dramatic fall in the prices of raw materials, and by the burden of their debt.
Is it normal that the poor countries should be forced to refund every year more than the new amounts getting in? Can they ask their populations to produce more and more all the time while receiving an ever smaller share of the product of their work?
Remember when a procedure was set up in the early 1980s, when some countries in the Middle East had considerable surplus capital. Let us do it again, let us follow that procedure. Since the end of the Second World War, those circumstances have occurred several times. I hope your country as well as mine are willing to take a leadership role in this vast initiative which will lead responsible, industrial, advanced nations to understand that there lies the answer for themselves as well as for others to the great question mark of our time.
Of course, ladies and gentlemen, the future of our planet does not only depend on the capabilities of states to ensure an adequate economic growth for the world. That will not solve all the needs of mankind. That future depends even more immediately on their capacity to preserve peace.
I made some comments on the organization of markets, on the fight against monetary disorder, on the necessary assistance to the development of poor countries. But I would like to say a few words about peace.
Having been invaded three times in 75 years, France is very much aware of the drama this represents, I can assure you. I referred to the help of Canadian soldiers. I lived through World War II myself, and I was born during World War I. How could my generation not be essentially marked by this nearly cyclical return to confrontations which, in the case of Europe alone, were the signal of a tragic civil war from which we are barely beginning to recover!
Shortly after the second conflict my country became a signatory to the Charter of the United Nations and its underlying principles. As a permanent member of the Security Council, France never hesitated to support the international organization. She helped it fulfil its duties, she denounced encroachments upon the rights of nations and individuals, she contributed as required to the peacekeeping operations. On behalf of the United Nations, France is still present on sites where the strongest passions clash.
The fact remains that the ratio of military strength, especially between the two most powerful nations, has led to massive stocks of weapons and a dangerous imbalance.
Despite efforts, the disarmament negotiations have not made it possible to limit, let alone reduce the massive strategic

May 26, 1987
arsenals of the United States of America and of the Soviet Union.
The so-called ABM treaty, to this day the only major arms control agreement still in force, is the object of vigourous debates which make us fear it may be weakened and even disappear.
Only the negotiations on so-called intermediate nuclear weapons, which do not cross the Atlantic but can reach all European countries, now show some signs of progress. And I say loudly from this podium that France hopes they will be successful. Let us not forget, incidentally, that the object of disarmament is to increase rather than to decrease security, to maintain rather than to compromise balances.
Our hope is that an intermediate nuclear weapons agreement is only one step towards disarmament, a step linked with the strategic disarmament on one hand-some 11,000 nuclear warheads in the Soviet Union, 12,000 to 13,000 in the United States of America-a step linked with the strategic disarma-nent on one hand and, on the other, with the disarmament of conventional forces, chemical weapons, or any other kind of weapon of whatever range which may lead to confrontation. All this within the limits of control, of flawless verification, that is to say of full respect for previous commitments.
France, as you know, is not party to the ongoing negotiations. She was not asked to sit at the disarmament negotiation table. Had she been asked, she would have refused. Indeed, as long as the two major powers remain at the stage where they are now, with the number of nuclear warheads I just mentioned, before asking others, particularly Great Britain or France which do have weapons, of course, but barely one hundred or two hundreds, great progress would have to be accomplished. Such is the theme I developed before the United Nations in 1983. But my country, like her neighbours, simply has to be concerned over a conflict or over the ongoing disarmament negotiations. And if we aim to preserve our independent strategy of nuclear deterrent, upon which we believe our security rests, we want to add our efforts to those of others to reduce tensions.
Ladies and gentlemen, France lies only a few hundred kilometres from the world on the other side of this Europe cut in half, from Teheran to Yalta. With her immediate neighbours she founded a community, six at first, a specifically continental group, then nine, ten, twelve. This Europe, we would like it to be able to organize its economy, 320 million people, a wider market than that of the United States of America, much wider than that of the Soviet Union, a body of technical and scientific competence, larger than Japan's, a historical capacity not to dominate-for henceforth such words cannot apply to the world's future-but to guarantee the presence of each of the states and nations of which it is made up.
Such is our first choice, our first will, our first objective. We want to build Europe and we are dedicated to this end. We are confronted with many obstacles. I was a young parliamentarian in 1948, nearly 40 years ago, attending the first European Congress, three years after the end of World War II, a congress chaired by Churchill. The Germans were there, and in each of our families grief, sorrow, separation and suffering still marked our mind when they had not marked our body. And yet a few of us were seeking reconciliation, to begin by France-Germany reconciliation, to help the other nations of Europe. Building Europe as we are doing today is not to dream nor to project onto an unknown horizon the too well known difficulties we are experiencing today. Europe is our main objective, but not the only one. The other, as I have already said, is to contribute to world harmony, to make sure that France, a country which maintained a presence for so long in Africa and elsewhere, as it still does, but differently, uses every opportunity to bring cultures closer together. Hence the importance of La Francophonie.
By the way, I am coming back shortly to your country to take part in the second Francophone Summit, in Quebec City, next September. You will have seen much of me within two seasons, but I am not complaining and I am not expecting to return the following year to Ottawa, where the Seven will meet again according to the agreed schedule, under a somewhat systematic moira which makes us meet year after year, always to face the very same problems, but in different locations.
Europe, the francophone brotherhood, universal enlightenment through peace and development, all these issues bring me to say that I could not conclude these remarks before your Parliament without raising with you the issue of human rights. In doing so, according to a theme which I have often developed in my own country, I shall borrow a quote which was also used by Hemingway in the title of one of his major works, For whom the bell tolls: When a freedom somewhere in the world is lost, when the right of a man is denied, when a life is unfairly broken, the bell tolls not only for that individual, but also for all of us. The struggle for freedom which you may lead, together with a great many others, in your daily actions is consistent with the major battles which have been fought for centuries to liberate man and every individual in the states where freedom would be secured. That may also be part of learning about democracy; in view of the present state of the world and current trends, we have every reason to fear for freedom. How good it makes me feel to be able to say that in a forum of free men and women! It is certainly the secret reason behind this deep understanding which unites us, above and beyond our conflicts and quarrels. We are part of that family.
I am well aware of the problems you have to face in your own country, as you certainly are of those which are spreading in mine.
I am not forgetting the special duties of my country-I will stress them tomorrow and the day after-to that part of Canada which once belonged to France and which, to this day,
May 26, 1987

continues to reflect its culture, language and tastes. I send very warm greetings to all the men and women who are listening to me and who have lived and are still living that experience, but I fully realize that a country as great as yours needs to collect all its varied components to stand up and act.
The ideals which I have tried to define are in line with those expressed by the Prime Minister and make up our heritage- and when I say our heritage, I mean yours and mine.
Let us be proud of this heritage. Let us not try to impose it, but let us try to convince. If Canada and France are seen by the world to be taking together simple but necessary action, as they did in the past and as they will even more in the future, along the path which we have chosen, then a visit such as this will have its place in our destiny, one which our conscience dictates, one where friendship and brotherhood prevail, one which will see Canada and France as two countries and nations increasingly associated in their daily progression and able to propose to the world a few remedies to the ills of the world, a world which is concerned and dying, but also a world which is born in each of your regions, provinces, states, everywhere from east to west, and from north to south, a huge country where the future is being born. There are, at times, a few men and women lost in the immensity . . . but there are cities, large centres, an industry, a growing agriculture, there is hope everywhere and a capacity to overcome obstacles. Yes, you have a lot going for you, ladies and gentlemen. Let me tell you simply this, without trying to lecture anyone: Know how to harvest your grain and make your flour.
A country like France, an older country, which has suffered a lot and will suffer again, has also unlimited potential and opportunities, because everything remains to be done for the coming century. That is why I often ask my fellow citizens to unite, not to ignore their own differences-everyone is entitled to his or her preferences, and I have mine-but to unite every time it is necessary to stand for the country or for mankind.
Well, I said everything I wanted to tell you, ladies and gentlemen, 1 would have liked, not to speak much longer, but to participate in a much broader exchange. I was very gratified by the warm welcome from the Prime Minister whose speech was well structured and, moreover, delivered in two languages. How pleasant it would have been, with you . . . Naturally, there is an opposition and a majority and I know both, ladies and gentlemen. I do not know which side is best. Depending on the circumstances in which I was involved, opposition or majority appeared to be better. But there is nothing worse than speaking for others. You are a sovereign country... How pleasant it would have been to be able to talk with you, with each of you, to become a parliamentarian again for a short while, lose probably this magnificient unanimity . . . But let us not lose it, ladies and gentlemen. 1 am through. Thank you for your warm welcome. Long live Canada! Long live France!

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Charbonneau (Speaker of the Senate):
subsubtopic: ADDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. President, Madam, we would very much have appreciated hearing more, because in this federal Chamber French is familiar to us and even custumary in the legal sense of the word, but it is a very rare occasion indeed to hear in this place a voice from France that is of recognized literary value, especially if it is that of the President. We were aware of that dual capacity in which'you spoke, and we were assured that the clarity and the contents of your comments would testify to it in this exclusive place where we are highly honoured by your visit. I thank you on behalf of my Senate colleagues.
We wish that your stay among us be surrounded by an atmosphere of cordiality, because our relationship with your country could not be bound in formality. Our countries are unique, but so are our bonds, and this perhaps is what makes them more delicate on occasion.
Approximately one third of Canadians are culturally linked to France. Those indestructible bonds forged in the past have unfortunately not been paralleled in the economic field for reasons history tries to explain. As you yourself often suggested, we must on both sides strive to recreate those flows between our two worlds, and the impetus at least has been given. We know very well that in the area of international trade, you must reckon with a number of partners since you succeeded in that bold Common Market experience. Of course, that did not happen without many difficult adjustments. For our part, we would also like to offer you an enlarged market of continental scope.
As you know, we are negotiating with our neighbours down south, and the outcome is still uncertain. In the event of success, our language duality would be an asset for you to gain access to a North American market.
To come back to cultural exchanges, would you allow us, Mr. Speaker, in your quest of a multimillenial past, to visit with you the Solutre Rock in a lay pilgrimage? As I suspect that you do not miss the opportunity to enjoy the gifts of nature offered by Pouilly on the one hand and Fuisse on the other, you could count on us to also partake in that pleasure.
With the near bicentennial of your Revolution, I would like to recognize before the statesman you are what Canada owes France.

The outbreak of the French Revolution and the fear that disturbances would spread to Canada encouraged the British Government to institute a more liberal form of government in the colony. The Constitution Act of 1791 divided Canada into two colonies, Upper and Lower Canada, and provided each with an elected legislature. Although the Constitution was cautious in the democratic powers it conferred, it represented the first step in Canada's path to nationhood and eventual independence. In those days, toasts were drunk to the French Revolution at a banquet held to celebrate the coming into effect of that Constitution.

May 26, 1987

Mr. President, for your 1789 Revolution, for our cultural heritage, for the example set by your Pan-European economic expansion, for your eloquence here, may we express our deep gratitude.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ADDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. President, we are especially honoured to welcome the President of the Republic of France, not only as the leader of a great nation, but as a special friend of Canada.
Your visit marks an historic moment in the life of our Parliament. It is a reflection of the lasting friendship and special relationship binding our countries.

France is not only the ancestral homeland of million of Canadians, it is also a sacred land where our soldiers died to make on two occasions right and freedom triumphant.
The cultural heritage left by France in Canada is an essential constituent of our nation.
Our attachment to the strength and influence of the French language and culture in the world has been clearly shown in the Francophonie Summit as a privileged tool.
The action of parliamentarians complements government measures as could point to you our colleagues in this chamber
who actively take part in the proceedings of the International French-speaking Parliamentary Association.
The Canada-France Interparliamentary Association and France/Canada friendship groups include women and men who are eager to contribute to the strenghtening of bonds in all areas of activity.

Your visit to Canada, Mr. President, provides us with an unique opportunity to celebrate the deep friendship shared between France and Canada. It also serves as a means for us to explore ways of expanding our relations, particularly with respect to economic and trade matters and to seek common ground to respond to the challenges facing our two nations.
On behalf of my colleagues, I wish to reiterate how pleased and honoured we are in welcoming you and Mrs. Mitterrand in this Flouse. We ask you to convey our fraternal greetings to parliamentarians of your country and to all fellow citizens.
Thank you, Mr. President.
I now adjourn this meeting.
